description.summary: A female supernatural figure of Irish folklore — the bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound' — whose mourning cry, the keen, foretells the death of a member of certain Irish families.
description.full: The banshee (Irish: bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde — 'woman of the fairy mound') is one of the most widely-known figures of Irish folklore. She is a female spirit, traditionally attached to specific Gaelic Irish families (especially those whose surnames begin with Ó or Mac, indicating ancient Milesian descent), whose appearance or wailing cry — the caoineadh, or 'keen' — foretells the death of a family member. Descriptions vary considerably across the corpus: some accounts describe her as a beautiful young woman with long streaming red or fair hair, in a green dress beneath a grey cloak, with eyes red from weeping; others describe her as an old hag or a small shrouded figure beneath the trees; her height ranges from one to four feet. She often appears combing her hair, and a folk taboo forbids picking up a discarded comb in case it is hers. She is not malevolent: her role is to mourn, not to cause death. The figure is documented as far back as the 14th-century Irish chronicle Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh ('The Triumphs of Turlough', c. 1380), and is collected extensively in Lady Wilde's Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland (1887), W. B. Yeats's Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888), and the standard modern scholarly study, Patricia Lysaght's The Banshee: The Irish Supernatural Death-Messenger (Glendale Press, 1986). Closely related figures appear in other Celtic traditions: the Scottish bean nighe (washerwoman at the ford) and caoineag, and the Welsh cyhyraeth. The banshee remains a living element of Irish folk culture, with claimed encounters periodically reported into the 21st century.

etymology.origin: Modern Irish bean sí (older bean sídhe), from Old Irish ben síde — 'woman of the síd', the fairy mound; síd / síde is the Old Irish word for the prehistoric burial mounds inhabited by the Aos Sí (people of the mounds).
etymology.meaning: 'Woman of the fairy mound'; by extension, a female supernatural mourner.
etymology.first_use: Old and Middle Irish prose; the 14th-century chronicle Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh (c. 1380) is among the early prose attestations of a banshee-like figure prophesying death.

taxonomy.variant: Irish bean sí (canonical); Scottish bean nighe / caoineag; Welsh cyhyraeth

related_phenomena.name: Bean nighe
related_phenomena.description: Scottish Highland washerwoman at the ford — washes the grave-clothes of those about to die.

related_phenomena.name: The Morrígan
related_phenomena.description: Old Irish goddess of war and fate; sometimes appears as a death-foretelling washerwoman at the ford in early Irish saga.

related_phenomena.name: Lhiannan-shee
related_phenomena.description: Manx fairy-lover; another Aos Sí figure.

features.description: Most depictions emphasise long red, fair, or silver hair, often unbound and floating.
Eyes red from continuous weeping are a recurring detail.
A common Irish costume: green gown beneath a grey or ash-coloured cloak.
Frequently described combing her hair; folk taboo against picking up roadside combs.
Reports range from a tall stately woman to a small (1-4 ft) shrouded figure.
May appear as an old crone (a 'hag of the air') in some accounts.

physical.morphology: An anthropomorphic female figure, varying widely from beautiful young woman to ancient hag; sometimes a tall stately apparition, sometimes a small shrouded figure beneath the trees.

abilities.description: Produces the caoineadh — a high, mournful supernatural cry — that foretells a family member's imminent death.
Bound to specific Irish families (especially Ó and Mac surnames), following them across distance and emigration.
Knows of an impending death sometimes before news of it has travelled to the family.
Can be seen as well as heard, often combing her hair near a stream or on a road.

habitat_preference: near family home of attached lineage
patterns: Appears in advance of a family member's death
Sometimes appears in groups of three (multiple banshees) at the death of a great person
Activity strongly nocturnal, especially in the hours before dawn
Travels with her family across geographic distance and emigration

range.description: Native to Ireland; cognate figures across the Celtic-speaking world (Scotland, Wales, Isle of Man). With the Irish diaspora the banshee tradition has been carried to North America, Australia, and other Anglophone regions.

first_recorded.source: Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh ('The Triumphs of Turlough') — Irish chronicle of the early 14th century containing what is widely regarded as one of the earliest prose attestations of a banshee figure (Aibhinn / Aoibheall foretelling death).

peak_activity_periods.description: Banshee firmly embedded in Irish family tradition, attached to specific lineages.
Major folkloric collections by Lady Wilde (1887), W. B. Yeats (1888), Lady Gregory (1920) record extensive banshee testimony.
Modern academic study (Lysaght, 1986) and ongoing reported encounters.

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Christian Irish tradition of the Aos Sí (the 'people of the mounds') and of female deities of fate, sovereignty, and battle. Closely linked to the Irish keening (caoineadh) tradition of female ritual lamentation at funerals.
origins.earliest_accounts: Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh (c. 1380) and other Irish chronicles. Patrick Logan and Patricia Lysaght cite Old Irish saga material in which female supernatural figures (e.g. Aoibheall of the Dál gCais; Cliodhna of the Tuatha Dé Danann) act as death-omen messengers.
origins.folklore_connections: Tied to Aoibheall, Cliodhna, and other Aos Sí women in Irish saga; cognate with the Scottish bean nighe and caoineag and the Welsh cyhyraeth.

timeline.event: Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh — Irish chronicle of the wars of Turlough O'Brien — describes a supernatural female figure (Aoibheall) foretelling the death of a Dál gCais king.
timeline.significance: Among the earliest documented prose accounts of a banshee-type figure.

timeline.event: The death of Edmund Mac Sweeney is preceded, according to family tradition, by the keening of a banshee — referenced in early modern Irish chronicles.
timeline.source: Patricia Lysaght, The Banshee (1986), and earlier Annals of the Four Masters references.

timeline.event: Lady Jane Wilde publishes Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland.
W. B. Yeats publishes Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry, with banshee material.
timeline.significance: Anchors banshee folklore in the literary revival.
timeline.source: Yeats, Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888).

timeline.event: Lady Gregory publishes Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland, with extensive collected banshee testimony.
timeline.source: Lady Gregory, Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland (1920).

timeline.event: Patricia Lysaght publishes The Banshee: The Irish Supernatural Death-Messenger (Glendale Press, Dublin).
timeline.significance: Standard modern scholarly study based on Irish Folklore Commission archive material.

history.modern_era: The banshee remains a living element of Irish folk culture, with periodic claimed encounters, especially within Irish-descended families abroad. She is a major reference point in Irish-themed popular culture — film, fantasy fiction, music, and video games — and is the subject of continuing ethnographic and literary study, especially of the keening tradition with which she is bound up.

documentary.name: Caithréim Thoirdhealbhaigh
documentary.description: Irish chronicle of the wars of Turlough O'Brien describing Aoibheall foretelling the death of a Dál gCais king — among the earliest prose attestations of a banshee-type figure.

documentary.description: Major Victorian compilation of Irish folkloric material with extensive banshee accounts.
documentary.source: Wilde, Lady (Jane Francesca Agnes), Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland (1887).

documentary.name: Patricia Lysaght — The Banshee: The Irish Supernatural Death-Messenger
documentary.description: Standard modern scholarly study, drawing on the Irish Folklore Commission archives.
documentary.source: Lysaght, P., The Banshee (Glendale Press, Dublin, 1986), ISBN 978-0907606215.

paranormal.name: Surviving Aos Sí ancestral / fate-spirit
paranormal.description: Within Irish tradition, the banshee is a real supernatural figure of the Otherworld — a daughter of the Aos Sí — attached to a specific family lineage and concerned with the fate of its members.

scientific.name: Misidentified animal cries
scientific.description: Many keening reports have been attributed to vixens, barn owls, foxes, and other nocturnal animals whose calls can sound human-like at distance.
evidence_cited: Documented similarity of barn-owl and vixen vocalisations to human screams

skeptical.name: Folkloric and literary construction
skeptical.description: Modern folklorists treat the banshee as a culturally constructed figure rooted in pre-Christian fairy belief and the Irish keening tradition, with no claim to material existence.

traditions: Irish keening (caoineadh) tradition of female ritual lamentation
Family-attached death-omen tradition (Ó and Mac surnames)
Scottish bean nighe / caoineag cognate tradition
stories: Aoibheall foretelling the death of Brian Boru's heir at the Battle of Clontarf (1014) in later traditions
Death of Edmund Mac Sweeney (1602) preceded by banshee keening
Numerous family-tradition accounts collected by Lady Wilde (1887), Yeats (1888), Lady Gregory (1920), and the Irish Folklore Commission
folklore.beliefs: Treated as a real but rarely encountered supernatural figure attached to specific Irish families; she does not cause death but mourns it in advance. Hearing her keen is taken as warning rather than threat.
